change_summary: prune_retention.py v1: fixed retention rules plus a --target-bytes rolling mode that deletes oldest-first until the mission root is under a target
expected: Rolling mode may relax the keep-N floors when the mission root is over budget, but must never leave the loop without a training window: at least one shuffleddata dir and at least one selfplay generation survive, and no selfplay generation is removed while a retained shuffleddata dir could still reference its rows.
observed: On the synthetic tree, `prune_retention.py --root $T --target-bytes 2000000` planned 6 paths / 900000 B, verbatim: 'WOULD-REMOVE 200000 B .../loop/selfplay/gen3', 'WOULD-REMOVE 200000 B .../loop/selfplay/gen4', 'WOULD-REMOVE 200000 B .../loop/selfplay/gen5', 'WOULD-REMOVE 100000 B .../loop/shuffleddata/20260904-000000', 'WOULD-REMOVE 100000 B .../loop/shuffleddata/20260905-000000', 'WOULD-REMOVE 100000 B .../loop/shuffleddata/20260906-000000' - i.e. all three surviving selfplay generations and all three retained shuffle windows. The plan was a dry run, so nothing was deleted.
root_cause: The rolling loop iterated a single pool of (mtime, path) over shuffleddata and selfplay together and applied only two guards: a shuffleddata survivor count computed against shuf_all (which includes the young dir, so it permitted all old dirs to go) and a selfplay guard comparing each generation's mtime against oldest_retained_shuf computed BEFORE the rolling deletions. It never consulted the fixed keep-N floors, so the generations the fixed rule had deliberately kept became free candidates.
fix_hypothesis: Split rolling mode into two ordered passes with explicit hard minima that are separate constants from the keep-N floors: first drop shuffle windows oldest-first down to ROLLING_MIN_SHUFFLE_DIRS = 1 survivor, then RECOMPUTE the oldest retained window from the post-pass state and only then drop selfplay generations older than it, down to ROLLING_MIN_SELFPLAY_GENERATIONS = 1; warn and stop rather than crossing either minimum.

ROOT CAUSE, reproduced here in the BEFORE columns of scenarios K and L: the first repair's EXIT trap made finalize() run on paths it had never run on before, and one of those paths is the chain's NORMAL end. Slurm ends every healthy link at --time by signalling the step with SIGTERM (SIGKILL follows KillWait 30 s later) and bash 5.1.8 runs the EXIT trap on SIGTERM, so finalize was called with no way to tell that end from an outcome of the cycle: with the process group signalled together it saw rc 0 and booked 'clean exit -- failcount reset to 0', wiping a genuine failure count (K6 shows 2 -> 0); with the child signalled first it saw rc 143 and booked 'failure -- failcount now 1/3', so three ordinary walltime rollovers would trip the breaker and scancel a live chain. A missing classification, not a wrong constant: the fix adds the third class rather than tuning the counter. Second conjunct, same function: finalize keyed a deliberate storage stop on the exit code 3 alone, while the loop writes $BASEDIR/STOP before exiting 3 (synchronous_loop_9x9.sh:245-246), so any stage that happened to exit 3 under bash -e ended the chain silently and uncounted; STOP is now the discriminator. Two design notes recorded for the validator. (1) The loop is deliberately NOT put in its own process group: bash defers a trap handler until the foreground command it is waiting on returns, so with the TERM trap installed the wrapper outlives the loop by construction (probe P, and K1-K3), while a separate group would only hide the loop from a group signal that slurmstepd's cgroup tracking reaches anyway. (2) The 128+15 inference is guarded by KTG_MIN_RUNTIME_SECONDS, so a stage that returns 143 within the first minutes of a link is still counted as the crash it is; a time-limit kill cannot arrive that early. Residual, recorded as [OPEN] in the candidate rows: a loop that returns 143 after a long healthy run for its own reasons is booked as a scheduler termination and the chain continues, bounded by KTG_MAX_CHAIN=200 and visible in sacct.
